intro: Hi! In this lesson you'll learn what comes after verbs like want and enjoy: I want to go home, but I enjoy swimming. You'll also learn to say why you do something with to: I go to the bank to get money. Warm-up: what do you want to do this weekend?
teachingNotes: When two verbs come together, the first verb decides the form of the second. want, need, would like, hope, plan, decide, learn + to + base form (I want to go home). enjoy, finish, don't mind + -ing (I enjoy swimming). There is no reliable meaning rule: present them as two short lists to memorise, each verb learnt with its partner (want to, enjoy -ing). The soft memory aid (to verbs look forward to something not done yet; -ing verbs talk about the activity itself) may help, but never sell it as a rule.

Common errors: *'I want go home' (Indonesian 'mau pulang' has nothing between the two verbs), *'I enjoy to swim' (Indonesian 'senang berenang' / 'menikmati berenang'), *'She want to go' and *'She wants to goes': only the first verb takes -s, and after to always the base form. Negatives and questions: don't / doesn't want to, Do you need to ...?

like, love and hate take both forms with no real difference here (I like swimming = I like to swim): accept both and never test them as either-or. But would like takes only to (I'd like to book a table, never *'I'd like booking'). mind = keberatan; keep it to 'don't / doesn't mind + -ing' at this level.

Purpose: to + base form answers Why? (I go to the bank to get money. Why do you go to the bank? — To get money.). Indonesian 'untuk' leads to *'for get money'. for + noun is fine (for lunch, for money, for my son); for + verb is not. Point out the two different to's in one sentence: to the bank = ke (place), to get = untuk (purpose).

Limits: use only present simple, present continuous, can, was/were and would like. No past simple (decided, went), no will, no going to, no present perfect. decide works in habits here (Every year, many people decide to learn English). Don't teach verbs that change meaning with to/-ing (stop, remember, try, forget), start/begin, 'in order to', or 'need + -ing' (the car needs washing). -ing spelling is as in the A1 lesson (writing, swimming).

keyPoints.title: Verb + to: want, need, hope, decide
keyPoints.explanation: Some verbs are followed by to + the base form of the next verb (the plain verb with no -s or -ing: go, buy, eat): want, need, would like, hope, plan, decide, learn. Indonesian 'mau pulang' has nothing between the two verbs; English needs to: I want to go home. Only the first verb takes -s: She wants to go.

examples.id: Sari berharap bisa bekerja di Singapura suatu hari nanti.

examples.en: Every year, many people decide to learn English.
examples.id: Setiap tahun, banyak orang memutuskan untuk belajar bahasa Inggris.

id.title: Kata kerja + to: want, need, hope, decide
id.explanation: Beberapa kata kerja diikuti to + bentuk dasar kata kerja berikutnya (kata kerja polos tanpa -s atau -ing: go, buy, eat): want, need, would like, hope, plan, decide, learn. 'Mau pulang' dalam bahasa Indonesia tidak punya kata apa pun di antara dua kata kerjanya; bahasa Inggris perlu to: I want to go home. Hanya kata kerja pertama yang diberi -s: She wants to go.

keyPoints.title: Verb + -ing: enjoy, finish, don't mind
keyPoints.explanation: enjoy (senang, menikmati), finish (selesai) and don't mind (tidak keberatan) are followed by verb + -ing: I enjoy swimming, not 'I enjoy to swim'. like, love and hate can take both: I like swimming = I like to swim. But would like takes only to: I'd like to swim.

examples.en: Dimas enjoys playing football with his friends.
examples.id: Dimas senang bermain sepak bola dengan teman-temannya.

examples.en: When I finish eating, I wash my plate.
examples.id: Kalau sudah selesai makan, saya mencuci piring saya.

examples.en: My mother doesn't mind cooking for ten people.
examples.id: Ibu saya tidak keberatan memasak untuk sepuluh orang.

id.title: Kata kerja + -ing: enjoy, finish, don't mind
id.explanation: enjoy (senang, menikmati), finish (selesai) dan don't mind (tidak keberatan) diikuti kata kerja + -ing: I enjoy swimming, bukan 'I enjoy to swim'. like, love dan hate bisa memakai keduanya: I like swimming = I like to swim. Tapi would like hanya memakai to: I'd like to swim.

keyPoints.title: to = untuk: saying why
keyPoints.explanation: To say why you do something (the purpose), use to + base form: I go to the bank to get money. It answers Why?: Why do you go to the bank? — To get money. Indonesian 'untuk' tempts learners to say 'for get money', but for comes before a noun (for lunch), never before a verb.

examples.en: I go to the bank to get money.
examples.id: Saya ke bank untuk mengambil uang.

examples.en: Rina is learning English to get a job in a hotel.
examples.id: Rina sedang belajar bahasa Inggris untuk mendapat pekerjaan di hotel.

examples.en: I go to the warung for lunch.
examples.id: Saya ke warung untuk makan siang.

id.title: to = untuk: menjelaskan tujuan
id.explanation: Untuk menjelaskan kenapa kamu melakukan sesuatu (tujuannya), pakai to + bentuk dasar: I go to the bank to get money. Ini menjawab Why?: Why do you go to the bank? — To get money. Kata 'untuk' membuat banyak orang bilang 'for get money', padahal for dipakai sebelum kata benda (for lunch), tidak pernah sebelum kata kerja.

blocks.text: Sometimes two verbs come together: *I want* + *go home*. A **verb** is an action word (*go, eat, buy, work*). When two verbs meet, the **first verb decides** the form of the second one. After **want, need, would like, hope, plan, decide** and **learn**, use **to + the base form**. The **base form** is the plain verb as you find it in the dictionary, with no -s and no -ing: *go, buy, work*. Grammar books call *to go, to buy* the **to-infinitive**; you only need to remember: **to + base form**.

id.text: Kadang dua kata kerja muncul berurutan: *I want* + *go home*. **Kata kerja** adalah kata untuk kegiatan (*go, eat, buy, work*). Kalau dua kata kerja bertemu, **kata kerja pertama menentukan** bentuk kata kerja kedua. Setelah **want, need, would like, hope, plan, decide** dan **learn**, pakai **to + bentuk dasar**. **Bentuk dasar** adalah kata kerja polos seperti di kamus, tanpa -s dan tanpa -ing: *go, buy, work*. Buku tata bahasa menyebut *to go, to buy* sebagai **to-infinitive**; kamu cukup ingat: **to + bentuk dasar**.

rows.id: Saya mau pulang.

blocks.text: Indonesian puts two verbs side by side: *mau pulang, perlu tidur, berharap bisa kerja*. English needs **to** between them: I want **to** go home, not 'I want go home'. Indonesian sometimes has *untuk* here (*memutuskan untuk belajar*) and sometimes nothing (*mau pulang*), but in English the **to** is always there after these verbs.

id.text: Bahasa Indonesia menaruh dua kata kerja berdampingan: *mau pulang, perlu tidur, berharap bisa kerja*. Bahasa Inggris perlu **to** di antaranya: I want **to** go home, bukan 'I want go home'. Bahasa Indonesia kadang memakai *untuk* di sini (*memutuskan untuk belajar*) dan kadang tidak ada apa-apa (*mau pulang*), tapi dalam bahasa Inggris **to** selalu ada setelah kata kerja ini.

blocks.text: Only the **first** verb changes. With he / she / one person: Rina **wants to go**, not 'Rina want to go' or 'Rina wants to goes'. After **to**, always the base form. Negative: I **don't want to** cook tonight. Budi **doesn't need to** work today. Question: **Do you want to** come?

id.text: Hanya kata kerja **pertama** yang berubah. Dengan he / she / satu orang: Rina **wants to go**, bukan 'Rina want to go' atau 'Rina wants to goes'. Setelah **to**, selalu bentuk dasar. Negatif: I **don't want to** cook tonight. Budi **doesn't need to** work today. Pertanyaan: **Do you want to** come?

blocks.prompt: My phone is almost dead. I need ___ it.
blocks.explain: need is followed by to + base form: I need to charge it. 'I need charge it' has no to, and need doesn't take -ing here.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: My phone is almost dead. I need ___ it.
id.explain: need diikuti to + bentuk dasar: I need to charge it. 'I need charge it' tidak punya to, dan need tidak memakai -ing di sini.

id.title: Kata kerja + to: want, need, hope ...

blocks.text: After **enjoy** (senang, menikmati), **finish** (selesai) and **don't mind** (tidak keberatan), use the **-ing form**: the verb with -ing on the end (*swimming, playing*). You know this pattern from *I like swimming*. The spelling is the same as before: read → reading, write → writing (drop the e), swim → swimming (double m). **Mind** is almost always used with *don't / doesn't* or in a question: I **don't mind** walking = it's OK for me to walk.

id.text: Setelah **enjoy** (senang, menikmati), **finish** (selesai) dan **don't mind** (tidak keberatan), pakai **bentuk -ing**: kata kerja dengan akhiran -ing (*swimming, playing*). Kamu sudah kenal pola ini dari *I like swimming*. Ejaannya sama seperti sebelumnya: read → reading, write → writing (buang e), swim → swimming (m digandakan). **Mind** hampir selalu dipakai dengan *don't / doesn't* atau dalam pertanyaan: I **don't mind** walking = saya tidak keberatan jalan kaki.

rows.en: Dimas enjoys playing football with his friends.
rows.id: Dimas senang bermain sepak bola dengan teman-temannya.

rows.en: When I finish eating, I wash my plate.
rows.id: Kalau sudah selesai makan, saya mencuci piring saya.

rows.en: My mother doesn't mind cooking for ten people.
rows.id: Ibu saya tidak keberatan memasak untuk sepuluh orang.

rows.en: I love dancing. = I love to dance.
rows.id: Saya suka sekali menari.

blocks.text: Indonesian *senang berenang* or *menikmati berenang* doesn't change the verb, so many learners write 'I enjoy to swim'. After **enjoy, finish** and **don't mind** there is **never** to: I enjoy **swimming**. After *enjoy* you can also put a noun: I enjoy **music**.

id.text: *Senang berenang* atau *menikmati berenang* dalam bahasa Indonesia tidak mengubah kata kerjanya, jadi banyak orang menulis 'I enjoy to swim'. Setelah **enjoy, finish** dan **don't mind** **tidak pernah** ada to: I enjoy **swimming**. Setelah *enjoy* kamu juga bisa menaruh kata benda: I enjoy **music**.

blocks.text: **like, love, hate**: both forms are correct and mean the same here: **I like swimming** = **I like to swim**. So you never need to choose for these three. But **would like** takes only **to**: I'd like **to** swim, not 'I'd like swimming'.

id.text: **like, love, hate**: kedua bentuk benar dan artinya sama di sini: **I like swimming** = **I like to swim**. Jadi untuk tiga kata ini kamu tidak perlu memilih. Tapi **would like** hanya memakai **to**: I'd like **to** swim, bukan 'I'd like swimming'.

id.title: Kata kerja + -ing: enjoy, finish, don't mind

blocks.text: There is **no simple rule** that tells you which verbs take **to** and which take **-ing**. English speakers just know them, so the best way is to **learn the two lists by heart**, like new words. Learn each verb together with its partner: *want to*, *enjoy -ing*.

id.text: **Tidak ada aturan sederhana** yang memberi tahu kata kerja mana yang memakai **to** dan mana yang memakai **-ing**. Penutur bahasa Inggris hafal begitu saja, jadi cara terbaik adalah **menghafal dua daftar ini**, seperti kosakata baru. Hafalkan setiap kata kerja bersama pasangannya: *want to*, *enjoy -ing*.

blocks.text: A small help (not a rule!): many **to** verbs look forward to something you haven't done yet: you *want, need, hope, plan, decide* **to** do it. The **-ing** verbs talk about the activity itself: you *enjoy* it, *finish* it, *don't mind* it. If you're not sure, check the list.

id.text: Sedikit bantuan (bukan aturan!): banyak kata kerja **to** melihat ke depan, ke sesuatu yang belum kamu lakukan: kamu *want, need, hope, plan, decide* **to** melakukannya. Kata kerja **-ing** membicarakan kegiatannya sendiri: kamu *enjoy*, *finish*, *don't mind* kegiatan itu. Kalau ragu, lihat daftarnya.

options: I enjoy to dance at weddings.
We hope to see you in Bandung.
She wants going to the beach.
blocks.explain: hope + to + base form: We hope to see you. enjoy takes -ing (I enjoy dancing), and want takes to (She wants to go).

id.explain: hope + to + bentuk dasar: We hope to see you. enjoy memakai -ing (I enjoy dancing), dan want memakai to (She wants to go).

blocks.text: To say **why** you do something (the **purpose**), use **to + base form**: I go to the bank **to get** money. It answers a *Why?* question, and the short answer starts with *To*: *Why do you go to the bank? — To get money.* In Indonesian you say *untuk*, so many learners say 'for get money'. That's wrong: in English **for** comes before a **noun**, the name of a thing or person (*for lunch, for money, for my son*). Before a **verb**, use **to**.

id.text: Untuk mengatakan **kenapa** kamu melakukan sesuatu (**tujuannya**), pakai **to + bentuk dasar**: I go to the bank **to get** money. Ini menjawab pertanyaan *Why?*, dan jawaban singkatnya dimulai dengan *To*: *Why do you go to the bank? — To get money.* Dalam bahasa Indonesia kita bilang *untuk*, jadi banyak orang bilang 'for get money'. Itu salah: dalam bahasa Inggris **for** dipakai sebelum **kata benda**, yaitu nama benda atau orang (*for lunch, for money, for my son*). Sebelum **kata kerja**, pakai **to**.

rows.en: I go to the bank to get money.
rows.id: Saya ke bank untuk mengambil uang.

rows.en: Pak Hasan works on Saturdays to earn extra money.
rows.id: Pak Hasan bekerja hari Sabtu untuk mendapat uang tambahan.

rows.en: Rina is learning English to get a job in a hotel.
rows.id: Rina sedang belajar bahasa Inggris untuk mendapat pekerjaan di hotel.

rows.en: Why do you get up at five? — To catch the first train.
rows.id: Kenapa kamu bangun jam lima? — Untuk naik kereta pertama.

rows.en: I go to the warung for lunch.
rows.id: Saya ke warung untuk makan siang.

blocks.text: Don't be confused by **two to's** in one sentence: I go **to** the bank **to** get money. The first *to* + a place = **ke** (*to the bank* = ke bank). The second *to* + a verb = **untuk** (*to get* = untuk mengambil).

id.text: Jangan bingung dengan **dua to** dalam satu kalimat: I go **to** the bank **to** get money. *To* pertama + tempat = **ke** (*to the bank* = ke bank). *To* kedua + kata kerja = **untuk** (*to get* = untuk mengambil).

blocks.text: Quick test for *untuk*: is the next word a thing or an action? A thing → **for**: I come here **for** the food. An action → **to**: I come here **to** eat. Never 'for eat', 'for get', 'for buy'.

id.text: Tes cepat untuk *untuk*: kata berikutnya benda atau kegiatan? Benda → **for**: I come here **for** the food. Kegiatan → **to**: I come here **to** eat. Jangan pernah 'for eat', 'for get', 'for buy'.

blocks.explain: This says why Dimas runs, so use to + base form: to stay healthy. for comes before a noun, not before a verb like stay.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: Dimas runs every morning ___ healthy.
id.explain: Ini menjelaskan kenapa Dimas berlari, jadi pakai to + bentuk dasar: to stay healthy. for dipakai sebelum kata benda, bukan sebelum kata kerja seperti stay.

suggestedQuestions: Why is it 'I want to go' but 'I enjoy going'?
Can I say both 'I like swimming' and 'I like to swim'?
When does 'untuk' become to, and when for?
Is there a trick to remember which verbs take -ing?
